problem.explanationEn: The text before the blank ("These ideas shaped ... pieces of music") and the text after it ("Kandinsky wanted viewers ...") are both independent clauses, so they need to be separated with a period. That makes A correct. B joins the two independent clauses with only a comma, which is a comma splice. C runs the clauses together with no punctuation at all, creating a run-on sentence. D adds an extra comma after the coordinating conjunction "and," and that comma doesn't belong there.

problem.explanationEn: The subject of the sentence is the plural noun "masks." The phrase "of these characters" only modifies it. That means the verb has to agree with a plural subject. Choice C, the past tense "made," has the same form for singular and plural subjects, so it agrees with "masks." It also fits the sixteenth-century, past-tense setting of the passage. Choices A, B, and D are all singular forms ("makes," "is making," "has made"), so they don't agree with "masks." Don't let the nearby word "characters" fool you: it is the object of the preposition "of," so it doesn't control the verb.

In the late thirteenth century, the Majorcan philosopher Ramon Llull devised what he called the Ars, a system for exploring religious and philosophical questions by combining a fixed set of basic concepts. Llull assigned letters to attributes such as goodness, greatness, and power, inscribed them on concentric paper wheels, and rotated the wheels so that every possible pairing appeared in turn. Llull himself intended the device as a tool of persuasion: he hoped that by producing every combination of divine attributes, it would lead Muslim and Jewish scholars to accept Christian doctrine through reasoning both sides already shared. Historians of computing, however, have increasingly pointed to the Ars for a different reason. Whatever its missionary purpose, the wheels carried out reasoning through a mechanical procedure, producing results by following fixed rules rather than relying on the insight of whoever turned them. It is this feature, and not Llull's theological conclusions, that later thinkers such as Gottfried Leibniz found worth developing when they imagined a calculus of thought.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

D adds "then," but "then" is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so the result is still a comma splice.

A는 쉼표만으로 두 독립절을 이어 쉼표 스플라이스가 된다. B는 아무 문장부호 없이 두 절을 붙여 무종지문(run-on)이 된다. C는 접속사 and 뒤에 쉼표를 두어 문장부호 위치가 잘못되었다.
problem.explanationEn: The text before the blank ("Silicone hydrogel lenses ... largely solved this problem") and the text after it ("their silicone component lets oxygen pass ...") are both independent clauses, each with its own subject and verb. A semicolon can join two independent clauses, so D is correct. A joins them with only a comma, which makes a comma splice. B puts no punctuation between them at all, which makes a run-on sentence. C puts the comma after "and" instead of before it, so the punctuation is in the wrong place.

hardJudge.note: 빈칸 앞뒤가 모두 독립절이며 세미콜론 연결(D)이 유일하게 적합. A 쉼표 스플라이스, B 무종지문, C 'and' 뒤 쉼표 오배치로 모두 배제됨. 한국어·영어 해설 결론 및 글자 참조 일치, 영어 자연스럽고 한글 없음. 하이드로겔/실리콘 하이드로겔 산소 투과 관련 내용은 사실과 부합. 독립절 연결 규칙 하나로 풀리는 전형적 easy 문항.

advisory.note: 두 독립절을 세미콜론으로 연결하는 기본 규칙 문항. 오답은 쉼표 스플라이스, 무종지문, 접속사 뒤 쉼표로 모두 전형적 오개념이다. 사실 관계(실리콘 하이드로겔 렌즈가 1990년대 후반에 도입되었고 산소 투과성이 높다)도 정확하다.
